title: Let the lender pace a key's traffic and absorb a throttle, and let tests inject provider faults through it
foundBy: session agent operating two eight-member campaigns side by side on one host, reading every member's own CLI session records and the lender containers' logs after both campaigns had ended
details:
**The observation behind it.** Eight members of two campaigns shared one provider key whose limit was 500,000 input tokens a minute. Their combined demand, summed from their own session records, had a median of 483,000 a minute for the whole of both campaigns, and cached input counted toward the limit in full. One member with a large context reached the ceiling by itself: an agent loop makes a request every ten seconds or so and each re-sends the whole context, so 145,000 tokens six times a minute is 870,000. Every member discovered the limit separately, by failing; the members with the largest requests lost the contention every time; and each failure cost a turn and, in a campaign, a recovery ladder that added to the load (the campaign ledger's SAC-034).

**The idea.** No member can see the total. The lender can: every call on a key already passes through it. It could hold a per-slot budget and **queue** a request that would exceed it rather than forward it, and when the provider throttles anyway, **wait the provider's retry-after and try again** instead of returning the 429. A CLI would then see latency and never a rate limit, for every CLI family at once, and two fleets on one key would become a queue rather than a fight. The budget has to be configured rather than guessed — limits differ by key and tier — and a stall watchdog downstream has to be able to tell a queued request from a wedged one, so queueing must be visible (SBX-046).

**The caution.** The proxy's present virtue is that it never reads a body: *"a stream passes through byte for byte and a request shape this build has never seen still works."* Pacing by tokens needs a size. The request's byte length is a usable proxy for it and keeps that property; parsing the body would not.

**The second half, which is cheaper and may be worth doing first.** Because every call passes through the lender, it is also where provider faults can be **injected** for tests: answer the next N calls on a slot with 429, with 503, with a hang, with a 401. That gives this repository and the campaign repository a way to prove what a turn driver, a wrapper and a recovery ladder do under each fault, on a throwaway sandbox, without spending a real campaign to find out. Every behaviour in SBX-044, SBX-045, SAC-034 and SAC-035 was learned from two four-hour campaigns because nothing cheaper could produce the condition.
